extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, scientists, and students of scientific method interested in induction and the discovery of forms/causes
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for conducting a true and perfect induction: which kinds of experimental/observational instances to collect and use (the 'prerogative instances'), plus supporting methodological components for discovering the ‘‘forms’’ or true natures of things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remaining helps of the understanding (methodological components)
rubrics_metrics.description: After the tables of first review, the rejection/exclusive table, and the first vintage, advance to the remaining helps of the understanding with regard to the interpretation of nature and a true and perfect induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists the components to be treated: 1) prerogative instances; 2) supports of induction; 3) correction of induction; 4) varying the investigation according to the nature of the subject; 5) prerogative natures with respect to investigation (what should be first or last objects of research); 6) limits of investigation (synopsis of all natures that exist); 7) application to practical purposes (what relates to man); 8) preparations for investigation; 9) ascending and descending scale of axioms. Use these as a roadmap for structuring inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solitary instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Solitary instances are those which exhibit the required nature in subjects that have nothing in common with any other subject except the nature in question, or which do not exhibit the nature in subjects resembling others in every respect except that nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These instances remove prolixity and accelerate and confirm exclusion: a few solitary instances can be as powerful as many. Examples: prisms and dews for color (they share only color with flowers/gems); veins of white/black in marble and variegation in flowers. Use solitary instances to deduce that a quality depends on optical effects or texture rather than intrinsic material. Use them to perform strong eliminations; they are particularly valuable for exclusion-based induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Migrating instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances in which the required nature passes toward generation (acquires existence) or toward corruption (is lost), i.e., instances showing the nature in transition or change (including increase/decrease).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They hasten and confirm exclusion and narrow the form because the form must be conferred or removed by the migration. They are useful in practice because they show the form coupled with what causes or destroys it, pointing toward efficient causes. The danger: they may falsely lead the understanding to attribute the form to the efficient cause (treating the cause as the form); remedy by proper exclusion. Examples: powdered glass or froth (whiteness appears on fragmentation/air inclusion), dissolving froth/snow (whiteness lost on melting), paper less white when moistened, illustrating role of air. Include migrations toward increase/decrease (e.g., paper when wet).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conspicuous instances (coruscations, free and predominant instances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances that show the required nature in its bare substantial shape and at its greatest degree of power, emancipated and free from impediments — the phenomenon in full vigor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They help reveal the form when the nature is unimpeded, but beware: whatever makes a show of the form is to be suspected and must be checked by severe exclusion. Examples: the thermometer as a conspicuous instance of expansive motion (heat) more clearly than flame, boiling water, or red-hot iron; quicksilver as a conspicuous instance of weight (showing gravity relates to quantity of matter rather than solidity). Use conspicuous instances to see the form at full strength but follow with exclusion tests to avoid deception from accompaniments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clandestine (twilight) instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances that show the required nature in its lowest or rudimentary state, subdued by contrary natures — the cradle or first rudiments of the nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They are valuable for discovering genera and common natures because they tend to lead to more general concepts (genera) whereas conspicuous instances tend toward differences. Look for faint or nascent expressions of a quality in small or mixed systems (e.g., bubbles, thin threads of water, froth and snow for consistency; magnet armed with iron as clandestine evidence of cohesion). Focus on small portions of bodies; these instances often reveal latent qualities that are hidden in bulk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutive instances (collective instances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances that constitute a species or lesser form of the required nature — groups of instances that collect into a common notion (particular or partial forms that assist in definition and division).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because real forms lie deep, these particular forms help by uniting groups of instances into workable species. But beware: do not stop inquiry after finding particular/species-level forms; prepare to search for the leading or great form (avoid prematurely assuming compound/divided nature). Examples (memory): constitutive instances include order/distribution, commonplaces of artificial memory, verse, impressions by passion, impressions when mind is pure (childhood/first occurrences), multiplicity of 'handles' (paragraphing, recitation), and anticipation; these constitute six lesser forms assisting memory. Examples (taste): constitutive instances show taste as partly internal smelling and an exquisite touch. Also use constitutive instances to distinguish momentary communications (light) from persisting ones (heat, magnetism). Use these to assist definitions, partitions, and local axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similar or proportionate instances (physical parallels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances that exhibit resemblances and connections of things in the concrete — physical analogies or parallels that show relations between bodies or parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They are not the strongest for discovering simple forms, but are valuable for disclosing the frame/structure of the world and may lead gently to higher axioms (e.g., organ-function analogies). Use them for anatomy of parts and for building axioms about construction of the world rather than for isolating simple natures. Examples: mirror and eye, ear and echoing places; roots and branches; gums of trees and rock gems analogy; fins of fishes and feet of quadrupeds; teeth and beaks; musical cadence and rhetorical surprise; mathematical postulate and logical syllogism. Restrict to substantial, not superficial or superstitious resemblances (avoid natural magic-style analogies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Singular instances (irregular or heteroclite)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances exhibiting bodies that are extravagant, separate, and little like other members of their species — unique or sui generis examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their use is similar to clandestine instances: they unite nature and help discover genera/common natures by forcing inquiry into exceptional cases. Do not stop at treating them as miracles; reduce their properties to forms or laws where possible. Examples: the sun and moon among heavenly bodies, the magnet among minerals, quicksilver among metals, the elephant among quadrupeds, certain unique sensations or letters. Use singular instances to correct understanding hardened by habit and to stimulate further investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deviating instances (errors of nature, monsters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances in which nature deviates or turns from her ordinary course — errors of nature or monstrous/abnormal objects in individuals rather than species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Like singular instances, they rectify the understanding and reveal common forms; they are more apt for practice and operative work because varying known species is easier than generating new ones. Use them to discover causes of deviation and to guide art toward producing analogous deviations. Collect monsters and prodigious births with rigorous selection and credible histories; beware superstition and unreliable reports (natural magic/alchemical fables).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bordering instances (participants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances that exhibit species appearing to be composed of two species or standing between two species — rudiments between one and another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They are rare but important for pointing out order and constitution of things and for suggesting causes of numbers and qualities of common species. Treat separately because they lead the understanding from what is to what is possible. Examples: moss (between putrescence and plant), some comets (between stars and meteors), flying fishes (between fishes and birds), bats (between birds and quadrupeds), biformed foetuses, mingled species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances of power (the fasces; masterpieces of art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Works or instances that are the most noble and perfect demonstrations of human art — masterpieces that show what man has achieved and which can be stepping stones to further discoveries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because making nature subservient to human needs is an aim, note and enumerate polished works of art: they make it easier to advance, adapt, or transfer them to nobler purposes. Artistic marvels often reveal modes of construction plainly (more so than natural miracles), and contemplation of them elevates understanding and suggests methods for producing new results. Use examples of perfected art as guides to possible operations and applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deriving a form: first vintage and operative definition (example: heat)
rubrics_metrics.description: Derive the form by comparing the first vintage (first review tables, rejections, and supportive instances) and state the form relatively (to the universe) and operatively (experimentally).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given for heat: from the first vintage derive the true definition: 'Heat is an expansive motion restrained, and striving to exert itself in the smaller particles.' Note that expansion is modified by tendency to rise and by being active. Operative definition: if one can excite a dilating or expansive motion in any body and repress that motion so it is only partially exerted, one will produce heat — testable by experiment irrespective of the body's material. Use both relative (philosophical) and sensible/operative (experimental) definitions to verify and apply the discovered form.
